Software supply-chain security has become one of the defining engineering concerns of the decade, because a modern application is far less a single artifact than an assembled graph of third-party dependencies, build tooling, container base images, continuous integration runners, and package registries that each represent an independent point of trust. When a team installs a package it rarely reviews, it inherits not only that package's code but the code of every transitive dependency, the credentials of every maintainer who can publish a new version, and the integrity of every mirror that serves the tarball. Attackers have learned that compromising one popular library propagates far more efficiently than attacking thousands of downstream organizations directly, which is why typosquatting, dependency confusion, maintainer account takeover, and malicious post-install scripts keep recurring. Effective defenses are unglamorous and layered. Pin dependencies to exact versions and record cryptographic digests in a committed lockfile so an unexpected change fails the build rather than silently shipping. Generate a software bill of materials for every release, and keep it queryable so that the response to a newly disclosed vulnerability is a database lookup rather than an archaeology project. Make builds reproducible and hermetic, run them on ephemeral isolated runners, and restrict the credentials available to a build step to exactly what that step needs. Sign artifacts and verify signatures at deployment time, so provenance is checked by machines rather than assumed by humans. Finally, treat the ability to publish as a production privilege: require hardware-backed multi-factor authentication for maintainers, review dependency updates with the same seriousness as first-party code, and monitor registries for packages whose names resemble your own.
